To improve medical image segmentation performance in semi-supervised scenarios, we've developed a straightforward post-processing method called "Consistency Reversal" (CR).  This technique involves a simple and efficient algorithm for fine-tuning an end-to-end fully convolutional network (FCN) after it has reached optimal training results.  By applying CR, we significantly enhance the utility of unlabelled data, achieving the highest ranking among seven comparison methods for both Inference-time and Model-training-time utility, according to our newly created metric called "usefulness at semi-supervised learning regime" (USSL).  When evaluated on four publicly available medical image segmentation datasets via USSL, we found that CR consistently excels over comparison methods.  Our results also demonstrate that CR is highly effective when applied to various FCN architectures, able to achieve state-of-the-art performance in abdominal multi-organ segmentation on the ABC-DR dataset and comparable results on the HPA-MaskRCNN dataset and the MedCoL dataset with Brain Hemispheres and Brain Tumors segmentation tasks.

In 2019, a significant breakthrough occurred when a two-qubit system was successfully used to demonstrate dichotomous quantum chaos by literally witnessing Liouvillean diffusion within the graph's Wigner function entropy, especially in the heisenberg xy spin model. This achievement was remarkable due to the extremely sensitive and detailed way it could track the graph's dynamics. Now we will build on this achievement by creating a graph-based neural network that can accurately identify the Heisenberg XY dynamics solely by analyzing the two-qubit system's Wigner function. In order to make this analysis more understandable, a neural network was trained to recognize the Heisenberg XY spin dynamics on all possible graphs, effectively creating a "fingerprint" database that can be used to compare the actual graph to its predicted counterpart, providing a quantitative measure of the neural network's confidence in its identification. When applied to the original scenario, this analysis revealed that the Wigner function's fingerprint matches the predicted dynamics only in the chaotic regime where the two-qubit system exhibits Liouvillean diffusion.

In statistics, working with a mixture model involves combining data from multiple distributions, each associated with a specific population. When trying to identify the original populations that the data came from, one must account for parameters associated with each population. This work focuses on estimating the average of a set of mixed parameters using an approach based on likelihood ratios, with the goal of applying this method to better understand sampling practices and limit biased sampling. The study discusses its advantages over other methods and provides empirical evidence for its performance in biased sampling cases.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based methods, which have been highly successful in predicting students' knowledge on online educational platforms. To further improve these models and make them more practical for real-world applications, it's essential to thoroughly evaluate them. Evaluations of deep learning-based knowledge tracing models often rely on limited and biased datasets, which can lead to models being overly fitted to specific data samples, resulting in poor performance on new, unseen student knowledge. To address this issue and provide more rigorous evaluations, a new approach is proposed that leverages transfer learning with knowledge tracing models as the source domain. This allows for the evaluation of deep learning-based knowledge tracing models as the target domain, enabling them to generalise better to new students. The proposed method is meta-learning based and can be used for both unsupervised and semi-supervised settings. To facilitate reproducibility and fair comparisons among different models and datasets, a comprehensive open-source Python framework called pyKT is also introduced, which includes the proposed method as well as additional tools for evaluating knowledge tracing models, including feature selection, ensemble methods and robustness assessments. By using pyKT, other issues with knowledge tracing models can also be examined, such as representations, robustness, generalisability and embeddings, across various educational platforms. To demonstrate the utility of pyKT, experiments are conducted on three publicly available datasets, showing that it's possible to evaluate knowledge tracing models at two levels: at the individual level, which reflects their performance on specific students

Given a complex manifold K, we investigate the linear space K[R] consisting of differential operators with smooth coefficients defined on K. By examining the properties of analytic sets within K, we can determine the conditions under which the span of K[R] is closed. If K contains no complex lines or planes, we prove that the span of K[R] is closed, providing a district example of this phenomenon. If the Jordan curve component boundary of a domain C is a Jordan curve, we also show that the span of differential operators defined on C with smooth coefficients is closed. Additionally, we provide an analogous result for the linear space of differential operators with smooth coefficients defined on a compact Riemann surface S, with the condition that S has no nodal components. If the boundary $\partial$D of a domain D is a compact surface with no boundaries, we also show that the span of differential operators with smooth coefficients defined on $\partial$D is closed.

One of the significant challenges in creating a general proof verification framework for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solutions stems from the diverse ways in which solvers express proofs. Various efforts have been made to standardize proof structures for specific theories, yet a comprehensive approach has yet to be established. Our proposal, namely Alethe, aims to provide a flexible and universal SMT proof structure, incorporating a range of proof constructs that can be applied across different mathematical domains, including linear real and integer, floating-point, Boolean, string, array, and bit-vector theories. The structure of Alethe can adapt to accommodate different proof styles and can represent both quantifier-free and full first-order logic constraints. We have developed the Alethe protocol and created a tool, namely Aletheizer, which can translate descriptions of proof structures into a format suitable for consumption by the verifier. Our hope is that Alethe will serve as a universal blueprint for proof structures, allowing researchers and developers to contribute specific implementations of the protocol that are tailored to the needs of particular solvers and applications. In this manner, we can move towards a unified proof verification framework, one that can be used with a wide range of SMT solvers.

As FL systems are increasingly used with mobile devices, there's a growing need to allow participating devices to contribute gradients without being constrained by synchronized updates. Despite the potential benefits of unconstrained gradient contributions, allowing devices to send gradients at any time based on local update rules can lead to inconsistent model updates and inaccurate gradient averages, posing significant challenges for FL implementations. To address this issue, we propose a novel asynchronous FL framework called Unconstrained Gradients in FL with Buffered Asynchronous Accumulation (UGA), which enables participating devices to contribute gradients at any time while maintaining model consistency and reducing estimation errors. By leveraging a carefully designed accumulation schedule and asynchrony buffer, the UGA framework provides a near-optimal solution for unconstrained gradient contributions in FL, with theoretical analysis showing that the algorithm achieves a satisfactory estimation accuracy with a well-controlled estimation error. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed UGA framework, we present and evaluate two variants, with simulation results indicating significant performance gains, particularly in scenarios with diverse device participation frequencies.

Recently, ASR systems have achieved significant accuracy with a focus on large-scale models. However, training such a system requires a substantial amount of data and significant computational resources. In this research, we explore a novel strategy called 'Rough-to-Fine ASR Transfer' where a base model with limited training data is used to generate intermediate features for a more complex model with ample data. Our results show that this method yields a 8.3% improvement in accuracy for a specific dataset. We also investigate the application of R2F to multiple languages and discover it can be mutually beneficial, leading to an average 6.1% decrease in error rate for both languages.

To enable long-term autonomous navigation for marine robots in dynamic and uncertain environments, it's crucial to model the time-varying nature of obstacles and attractors using their past histories. To achieve this, we propose a novel method that combines a sparse representation of attractors and a Gaussian process model of the surrounding environment, allowing for the prediction of future observations based on past data. We structure our model as a set of separate representations for the current and past time steps, using sparsity to constrain the representation of the current time step to only incorporate direct sensory input, and learn the parameters of the Gaussian process model using a sparse representation of the current time step. We further develop an online learning algorithm to update our model in real-time, using a sparse representation of the previous time steps to guide the update of the Gaussian process model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in a simulated navigation task, and show it can adapt to sudden changes in the environment, as well as learn from limited sensory input.

We've performed an expansion of the Einstein field equations to investigate a relativistic self-gravitating dual-fluid object within a nonisotropic setup, where two components, represented by fluids with different energies and pressures at each point, make up the entire object. This expansion allows us to re-write the Einstein field equations as a set of five nonlinear differential equations in curved space-time, solving these equations yields a complete picture of the object's structure, including its mass energy density, pressure, acceleration, and shift, across its volume. A thorough analysis of these solutions near the surface of the object, specifically in the non-relativistic limit, also provides insight into the object's behavior in this region. A numerical scheme is employed to solve the differential equations through an iterative process, and through this method, we've obtained solutions for various types of distributions, including static objects, as well as solutions for objects in both equilibrium and dynamical states, such as binary coalescence.

Recently, sequence-to-sequence based models have achieved superior performance in grammatical error rectification, but they often require massive amounts of data to train and tune, limiting their practical applications. This paper explores a domain transfer approach to adapt these models for new domains with limited resources, leveraging the knowledge gained from existing domains. A meta-learning framework is proposed, combining a training phase that implements domain-specific adaptations with a fast phase that transfers knowledge between domains. Theoretical analysis of this approach is supported by experimental evaluations on three datasets, showing that the proposed method significantly improves performance compared to baselines, especially when there's a significant domain difference.

The task of allocating non-divisible items to self-interested agents in a fair manner is a difficult problem, especially when considering the presence of strategic behavior. In this context, having a fair allocation does not guarantee a desire to cooperate, as cooperation can be problematic due to the presence of pure Nash equilibria that result in unfair outcomes for some of the players. In our work, we identify specific types of environments where all pure Nash equilibria are fair, by developing a framework that is based on a broad category of well-known methods for making allocations more equitable. The heart of our approach is a simple and intuitive idea: we divide the items into two distinct groups, with the easier items to allocate being placed in the first category, and the more challenging items in the second. The difficulty of the second group varies depending on the specific problem, but it can be understood in terms of a specific challenge it poses, such as items that cannot be fairly divided even in the presence of external power, or items that are associated with a specific order of precedence. We demonstrate the broad applicability of our framework by applying it to several well-known item allocation problems that have not been previously understood in this way. One of the problems we examined, the allocation of rewards in a second-price auction, may be considered a natural extension of our approach, as it places a specific constraint on the items that is reflected in the way the allocation is defined. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, allows us to observe the interstellar medium within H II regions in H alpha emission, revealing a distinctive "double-peaked" profile of the (Hα/Hβ) line ratio, attributed to a significant contribution from the nebula's continuum rather over expected values for H II regions. We propose this unusual feature could result from a very hot central star, possibly associated with a rare "hyper-constant" disc that heats up stars rather than just warm planetary bodies, potentially explaining the observed (Hα/Hβ) ratios. Alternatively, this ratio pattern may be caused by a combination of radiation from multiple young stars and a constant disk, leading to a need for further observational data to clarify the source of the (Hα/Hβ) ratios in H II regions of UGC 8839.

Using lattice QCD with two flavors of dynamical quarks, we investigate the correlation between quark and antiquark flavors in meson bound states. Our analysis focuses on the spatial distribution of correlation lengths within mesons, specifically examining how they vary in relation to quark flavors and momentum. Our lattice data reveals distinct patterns of correlation lengths in different meson species. In general, we find that mesons exhibiting significant quark and antiquark flavor correlations tend to have lower masses, and these correlations generally increase with rising momentum. Notably, our findings confirm that pions exhibit the greatest degree of quark and antiquark flavor entanglement among all mesons evaluated.

Accretion variability in young stars, like their protoplanetary disks, can provide valuable insights into the disks' behavior and potential planetary formation.  By analyzing data from the ACCINT grid, a collection of spectroscopic star mass accretion rates, a recent study identified a unique pattern of YSO XX Cha, located in the Chamaeleon complex, by examining the spatial distribution of its mass accretion rates.  Uniquely situated at the center of a double system, XX Cha exhibits irregular accretion behavior compared to other stars in the complex.  A comparison of its mass accretion rates to those of other young stars, also derived from spectroscopic data, using a new method that accounts for the effects of inclination and orbital periods, showed that the rates of XX Cha fall outside the usual range of accretion rates.  This result has implications for understanding the behavior of YSOs in binary systems and can be used to better understand the dynamics of YSOs with masses less than 0.5 solar masses.

Offline learning for multiple agents in a reinforcement learning setting with
limited data poses a significant challenge. Since many offline datasets contain
improper data, with most experience being outside of desirable policy bounds,
using standard offline methods can lead to poor results due to inclusion of
many negative experiences. Both state-of-the-art offline multi-agent methods and
standard offline methods include all experiences equally, which isn't ideal in
this case. We're introducing a novel framework called MAPT that focuses on the
useful data from successful training experiences. Based on this framework, we
develop a simple yet effective approach for learning from the successful paths
of multiple agents by using a shared critic and individual policy agents. The
successful experiences are identified based on a stable distribution of actions
derived from simple considerations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our
approach on challenging benchmark tasks by achieving the best known results in a
wide range of settings and scenarios.

Recently, MV images have gained popularity for their potential in assisting setup verification and patient positioning both inside and outside radiation therapy treatments. However, utilizing MV images requires aligning them with corresponding MV images taken after treatment, which are typically captured as part of the treatment process. This task, known as post-treatment MV-to-MV image registration or alignment, can be challenging due to factors such as respiratory motion, limited field of view, and distortion caused by megavoltage screens. In this study, a novel approach is proposed, where a convolutional neural network is used to align MV images with the help of kilovoltage images serving as additional guidance. The proposed method was tested on a dataset consisting of 50 2D images and 50 3D images, yielding alignment accuracy of 5mm in 2D and 7mm in 3D. Notably, the proposed method was found to outperform a traditional method using gradient of probability density models by approximately 1mm in both 2D and 3D cases.

When examining single-particle states, a crucial aspect is often overlooked – the role of entanglement in generating nonlocal effects. Most research focuses solely on bipartite entanglement, ignoring the significance of single-particle states in quantum nonlocality. However, the non-equivalence of single-particle states and bipartite entanglement has been demonstrated by the team from the University of Vienna. They achieved this by creating a genuine nonlocal effect in a single-particle scenario, utilizing a Mach-Zehnder interferometer and a beam splitter. The outcome shows that even when two parties share the same single-particle state, as prepared in this experiment, they are not necessarily able to generate a nonlocal effect through measurement. The condition for this effect to occur is that the state must be entangled when the system and its environment are considered together. The team's findings have the potential to advance the development of single-particle state-based quantum nonlocality, by moving beyond the study of bipartite entanglement.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding method has been presented, based on Gaussian mixture models (GMMs), which are trained using uplink signals from a mobile device to a base station. This approach allows for the construction of a codebook that adapts to varying channel conditions, which can lead to a 4-fold reduction in required feedback bits, compared to traditional methods, without sacrificing pilot transmission time. Further research demonstrated that by selecting the mean of the most relevant Gaussian component as the codeword, a 64-fold decrease in encoding distortion can be achieved, which leads to a gain of 3 dB in received signal power, compared to conventional methods.

Within Hofstadter models, in dimensions of three dimensions, in the presence of strong magnetic fields, in the range just beyond equilibrium, distinctive patterns of Wigner junctions and barriers can be formed using exact methods, with the behavior being controlled by the direction of tilt in the chemical potential and the strength of drive, and displaying unique characteristics, such as the formation of helical boundaries, and including results that exhibit topological properties just observable in three dimensions.

One of the key assumptions in superhump theory requires the disk to gradually lose mass at a constant rate to create 0.1 to 3.5 d orbital period lags in the H-alpha and other spectral lines. This assumption has been supported by observations of some stars but not others, and it remains unclear if it's a universal rule. This study used new and existing data along with computer simulations to study the superhump phenomenon in detail and discovered that the average orbital period increases more quickly in the later stages of the disk's completion, which can be explained by the distribution of orbital periods without needing to invoke variable Bondi mass loss rates.

We investigate the formation of nuclear star clusters at the hearts of giant galaxies by analyzing the mass limits and formation channels of these clusters. It is proposed that early star formation in these clusters could prevent gas buildup, leading to the formation of low-mass black holes via gas collapse or binary interactions. This process would result in a population of black holes with a mass range from 10 to 100 solar masses, primarily produced through binary interactions. Using a semi-analytical model, we simulate the formation of nuclear star clusters in a variety of galaxies and recover black holes in these clusters, even in the absence of stellar mass black hole binaries. This method allows us to recover black holes in these clusters, even in the absence of stellar mass black hole binaries. We then use this model to identify the most promising sources of gravitational waves produced by the coalescence of black holes in nuclear star clusters. These sources are primarily located in massive galaxies hosting bulges with a central stellar mass of 10 to the power 9 solar masses and are more frequent in galaxies with higher star formation rates. We also find that the most frequent sources of gravitational waves produced by the coalescence of black holes in these clusters occur in giant low surface brightness galaxies with low rates of satellite galaxies and occur with a frequency of about 2 per thousand years per galaxy, with a mass range of 20 to 50 solar masses and a merger rate of 3.5 to the power 4 per cubic megaparsec.

In Multi-Carrier Wireless Transmission, a scenario involving a source node, an eavesdropper, and a relay node with limited knowledge and a single data stream per subcarrier was analyzed. An AF relay transmission method was considered to ensure the security of data transmission. An optimization problem was formulated to maximize the number of subcarriers with strong encryption, considering that the relay node has access to partial channel information. An upper and lower bound was found to solve this challenging problem. An upper bound was achieved by assuming all subcarriers had full channel information available, resulting in an optimized solution for this case. Another upper bound was established by sorting the gain coefficients of each subcarrier in descending order. This led to a simple but less efficient solution. By comparing these two bounds, an algorithm was developed to solve the optimization problem efficiently.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform for evaluating virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, problem-solving, and natural language generation.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, with typical reinforcement learning training taking multiple days on a single GPU.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three popular text-based games, enabling training at an incredible rate of one million steps per second.
By applying innovative optimization techniques, TextWorldExpress achieves this remarkable speed on a single GPU without sacrificing accuracy.
In comparison to the original versions, TextWorldExpress trains for three times the number of episodes in half the time and successfully trains 25 million steps in just two days.
Our aim with TextWorldExpress is not solely to break records but also to make text-based training more accessible to the research community by making high-speed training available to everyone.
Our hope is that other game creators can learn from our optimization strategies, which can be applied to any text-based game, allowing the community to focus on developing more challenging and exciting games rather than getting bogged down in tedious technical details.

Deep neural networks, particularly LSTMs used in video recognition, experience slowdowns due to limited memory and high computational costs. This research addresses these limitations by designing an energy-efficient LSTM architecture for video identification tasks. A novel 'layer-merged' LSTM structure is presented, which combines input gates and memory cells to optimize computation and memory usage. To further enhance performance, a custom LSTM implementation was developed using a Co-Design methodology, incorporating a range of low-level hardware optimizations. The resulting LSTM, with a hierarchy of 3 layer-merged blocks, was found to provide significant improvements in memory usage, 1.4 times faster execution, and 12% increased accuracy in video identification tasks when compared to a non-merged LSTM. When applied to the LISA and GHGE video identification datasets, this energy-efficient LSTM achieved top-ranking performance among 12 competing models, with 96.5% and 94.6% accuracy respectively.

The convex hull criterion plays a significant role in identifying the ground state of a system in certain situations, particularly when applied to holographic conformal field theories. It ensures that the closest point to the ground state, using the Hamltonian as a distance metric, is part of the original convex hull of ground state operators. If the system is in a state of thermodynamic equilibrium, this condition is met. It remains unclear whether this condition is a fundamental requirement or a consequence of a specific setup. However, studies have shown that even when ground state operators are not in a state of thermodynamic equilibrium, the condition still holds, indicating it might be a fundamental property. Notably, an examination of a specific scenario, involving a system at finite temperature in an AdS-Schwarzschild black hole background, shows that even when the system is not in a state of thermodynamic equilibrium, the condition is met, although it is not a necessary requirement as it can be satisfied in other ways.

Given a Noetherian local ring (R, m) and an R-module of finite length, a tight Hilbert polynomial is defined to lack non-trivial zeros when evaluated at maximal ideal multiplicities. This concept is linked to the study of monogenic ideals in 2-dimensional local domains, specifically those containing a rational singularity, and it's shown that (R, m) possesses this property if and only if a specific F-invariant ideal has infinite depth.

Recent research highlights the significance of considering co-benefits in order to enhance the effectiveness of policies aimed at improving power supply diversity through the procurement of supplementary services. Studies have demonstrated that such policies have the potential to yield economic and environmental payback in local communities surrounding thermal power plants. In addition, it has been found that the impact of these policies can extend to neighboring markets where generators trade services freely. This research paper in question takes it a step further by exploring ways to refine such policies by accounting for the effects on neighboring markets and the resulting outcomes in those areas. It is hoped that by doing so, it will be possible to devise more effective strategies for promoting power supply diversity and mitigating environmental consequences and social injustices in local communities and surrounding markets through the procurement of supplementary services.

Consider the space of functions that map real numbers to real numbers, equipped with a certain norm. The article examines the decomposition of an arbitrary function, defined on a specific interval, in terms of its prime factors. It also investigates the properties of the composition of a set of functions, each defined on a separate segment, to obtain a function on the original interval. It is proven that if a function is decomposed into its prime factors as f ∘ g ∘... ∘ h, where each factor is defined on the interval (0, 1) or (1, 0), then it can also be expressed as a composition of the same form, with the same number of factors, each defined on one of the specified intervals. It is then shown that the iterates of a non-trivial function that maps real numbers to real numbers do not have a prime decomposition.

Recent studies have identified polar vortices in both Earth's and Mars' atmospheres that form during their respective solstices. Saturn's polar vortices were previously detected using the Cassini IFS instrument in the northern atmosphere, specifically in 2007 when they became prominent, and have not been observed since then. We used Saturn's infrared spectra obtained from the Michelson Interferometer for Remote Imaging Integration (MIIRI) on the James Webb Space Telescope to discover a spiral pattern of polar aerosols in Saturn's northern atmosphere that surrounds a newly formed vortex over the pole. Uniquely shaped, the vortex exhibits both curved arms and a central, cloud-free eye, with Saturn's newly formed northern polar vortex likely forming in the summer, making it the second known instance of a Saturnian polar vortex with defined latitudinal boundaries.

This work investigates solutions to the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation outside a convex boundary, specifically in the context of the energy problem for the PDE in question. A key aspect explored here involves the identification of conditions under which solutions with bounded energy can be confined within a specified region, without adhering to the assumption that the solution must eventually concentrate near the origin as time progresses. Rather, we consider the scenario where the solution exhibits an explosive pattern, with growing amplitude and shifting frequency over time. This research builds upon prior work by Bizoń, Dyskretović, and their collaborators, with the additional contribution of the current paper providing explicit bounds with respect to the geometric parameters of the obstacles in question.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic zero hypotheses are not required to establish the fundamental theorem regarding the equivalence of the Segre embedding and the smooth and regular composition of the rational representation of the symmetric group, specifically in the context of the minimal polynomial defined by the first F-regularity and the (m,n)-Differential Property.

We establish that for any graded collection of vector spaces, the linearization of its symmetric algebra has a well-defined extension to higher grades, resulting in a compatible chain of morphisms. This compatible chain can be viewed as a part of a larger, compatible chain of morphisms, whose target is the tensor algebra of the original vector space. This latter chain consists of a series of inclusions that form a chain of pushforwards in the category of graded modules, and whose image is composed of all modules that are generated under the action of the dual numbers, by the original vector space. As a consequence, the linearization of the symmetric algebra of a module can be precisely characterized as the module whose underlying space is the image of the action of the dual numbers on itself, when acted upon by the original module.

This informal note begins by illustrating some technical concepts, which include the re-normalization of orbital integrals from algebraic geometry and the application of certain technical properties related to compact groups. These properties were initially established by C. Mozo as a direct corollary of the results found in A. Connes', M. Shulman's, and E. H. Wigner's work. We also discuss some specific examples and related proofs.

Reconstructing a neutron star's surface density and composition is challenging but crucial for understanding nuclear matter's behavior at high pressures and temperatures. Despite the importance of this information, it's difficult to extract from observational data due to heavy contamination from electromagnetic radiation caused by scattering of X-rays on free electrons and nuclei. A novel method has been proposed where the scattered X-rays are used to determine the optical depth of the surface layers, and this information can be obtained from X-ray diffusion, specifically in the He-like and H-like spectra of the most abundant elements, particularly oxygen and carbon. This method can be tested with data from the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) and the X-ray Telescope (XRT) on board the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO), and it's anticipated that it will be possible to retrieve reliable information about the surface density of neutron stars with masses between approximately one and two solar masses using IXPE and SDO XRT. This will be a significant breakthrough, as it will be the first time it's been possible to obtain this kind of information from observational data, and it's expected to have a major impact on the study of dense matter, as it will be able to provide constraints on nuclear theories and help resolve the outstanding issue of neutron star radius uncertainty.

This research introduces a novel mixed finite element method, combining
traditional and hybrid techniques to model single-phase Darcy flow within
porous media featuring independent sets of fractures. Focused on a 2D $d$-dimensional space, we've developed a non-conforming finite element approach using polylagonal elements to represent fracture boundaries, and a corresponding hybrid variational formulation to solve the problem. A key innovation involves the use of consistent embedding methods, where fractures are considered as elements, and a key aspect of the formulation, the terms associated with fluid pressure at fracture boundaries, are automatically accounted for. A key benefit of this approach is the absence of need for fracture boundary condition enforcement, a common challenge in traditional methods. A series of numerical experiments are presented, demonstrating the effectiveness of this method in a range of scenarios, including those with significant differences in fracture and matrix fluid conductivity, and showcasing the method's ability to produce accurate and stable results even with a wide range of mesh types.

When employing Bayes factors to resolve model selection issues, several factors must be considered to ensure accurate and efficient results. We examine different workflow approaches to calculate Bayes factors using Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, either directly or via their relationship with marginal likelihoods. Our investigation covers three main calculation methods: the ratio of marginal likelihoods, bridge sampling, and proportion of allocated data, as well as two meta-estimators: the nested Bayes factor and Bayes factor Bayes factor. We outline a step-by-step procedure for selecting these methods and calculate Bayes factors for two models using both Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC) simulations and real-world data. Our results indicate that the proportion of allocated data and nested Bayes factor methods consistently yield accurate Bayes factor estimates for equal prior probabilities, whereas the behavior of these methods differs when prior probabilities vary. Our study is designed to aid researchers in choosing suitable methods to calculate Bayes factors for model selection, based on empirical data and various workflow considerations.

In our analysis of Twitter posts containing "by contrast" and similar comparative
expressions, we identified various semantic patterns, including both contrastive
and non-contrastive uses. Our study shows that many previous assumptions
about the inherent oppositional nature of these expressions are inaccurate.
Rather, their meaning is influenced by the context in which they are employed.
We have constructed a rule-based system to automate the examination of the
semantic implications of discourse markers, including those that indicate
contrast, and have utilized this tool to investigate the diverse meanings ascribed
to "by contrast" and comparable expressions, including its potential contrastive
and noncontrastive interpretations, across different genres of text, and
within the specific context of Twitter posts. Our research in this regard has
been applied to Twitter data, where we have analyzed the expressed intentions
behind the use of these expressions, and have made the tool, known as DiscSense
available to the public for further study and extension.

We investigate the structure of a specific class of low-rank matrix optimization problems, focusing on convex and non-convex cases and providing an exhaustive analysis of the problem's landscape from a Riemannian perspective. By converting a matrix optimization problem into an equivalent form involving a vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$, we establish that fixed-rank matrix optimization over the positive definite space can be treated as a type of convex or non-convex optimization problem in $\mathbb{R}^n$. We identify conditions under which the gradient of the objective function vanishes at all points, and analyze the problem's landscape as consisting of two distinct components: a flat surface surrounding a sphere, or a surface with an exponentially small narrow peak at the minimum point.

A recent study proved that every non-hamiltonian cubic bipartite graph can be edge-tinted with the number three, making it a necessary condition for a hamiltonian cubic bipartite graph to have a 3-edge coloring. This necessary condition was initially proposed by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990. A counterexample to this conjecture has been discovered – a hamiltonian cubic bipartite graph that requires a 4-edge coloring.

We investigated a model where two populations, one producing a continuous output and the other providing a price, evolve in a coevolutionary manner. The goal of both populations was to maximize their gains in a Cournot-style game, with the producer's gain being determined by the product of the set price and output, and the seller's gain being the product of a random output and the established price. We observed that a state of equilibrium could be achieved where the gain of one group was directly linked to reducing the gain of the other group. We identified three distinct types of evolutionary pathways that could lead to this state of equilibrium: one was characterized by a shift in pricing strategies accompanied by a shift in output, another by a shift in pricing strategies with a shift in output in the opposite direction, and the third was marked by no change in output but rather a change in pricing strategies. We discovered that this state of equilibrium was more difficult to achieve when the populations were not identical, as it required both a change in pricing strategies and a change in output, with the outcome being dependent on the specific evolutionary rates. We also found that this state of equilibrium could fail to persist if the populations were not identical, with the outcome being determined by the relative difference in their respective evolutionary rates. We further discovered that this state of equilibrium could fail to persist if the populations were not identical, with the outcome being determined by the relative difference in their respective evolutionary rates. Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and normal power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalent properties for a particular subclass of weighted directed graphs, which includes both weighted undirected graphs and directed trees. Additionally, when $\mathcal{D}$ is composed of two components - a tree as the underlying structure and the directions forming a cycle - we find that the normal and symbolic powers of $I(\mathcal{D})$ exhibit the same behavior, equivalently to the properties observed in [Theorem 1.1].

The introduction of activation interval supervision provides a precise justification for a key aspect of neural networks' behavior, which is crucial for validating the effects of stuck-line faults. Traditional analysis of neural networks shows that, in theory, all should follow a linear pattern when activated, yet in practice, many deviate from this standard. A study on eight different neural networks, trained to identify digits, reveals that only one, a simple network, adheres to this standard, with the remaining seven neural networks exhibiting non-linear characteristics, particularly in their output ranges. These ranges can vary greatly, from the simple network's less than 0.5 interval, to the largest neural network's interval of over 16,000. These findings serve as the basis for exploring the effects of stuck-line faults on these neural networks, particularly those with large output ranges, and how fault tolerance can be achieved through training, without sacrificing accuracy, as demonstrated by an example using a neural network with an output range of over 29,000.

This research paper presents an in-depth exploration of a novel, one-parameter variation of the Jordanian twist, which is derived from a specific type of Lie algebra extension. The authors illustrate the twist's conservation properties, demonstrating that the modified Jacobi identity and the commutativity of time evolution are both violated by a factor directly proportional to a specific Casimir operator. The proposed one-parameter family of the Jordanian twist can be viewed as a versatile tool that enables the construction of a broad spectrum of 2-parameter Lie algebraic deformed Hamiltonians, thereby offering insights into the underlying physics and providing a more accurate representation of the physical phenomena in question.

Constructing a shared semantic space across languages has been made easier by the vast amount of multilingual text available on the internet. This space serves as a foundation for various multilingual tasks and can facilitate communication and data exchange between languages. Although previous methods have successfully created shared spaces, they have limitations such as requiring word annotations and assuming equal distances between languages, which can hinder the quality of the space and restrict the choice of languages that can be used. In response to these challenges, we propose a novel approach that builds a shared space based solely on word embeddings and ensures the space reflects the internal structure of each language. The proposed method clusters words within each language and ensures the clusters are preserved in the shared space, allowing the space to adapt to the unique structure of each language. In order to preserve the structure of each language, we developed an innovative strategy that uses the distribution of words in the shared space and their clusters to update the space until it meets certain criteria. In experiments conducted on multilingual data, the proposed method outperformed existing approaches in terms of preserving the internal structure of each language and was found to handle languages with small amounts of data effectively. Furthermore, the method demonstrated its utility in enhancing the performance of multilingual tasks by conducting an experiment on word translation.

The initial production of mesons and baryons in high-energy collisions is influenced by various factors including the mass of the particles, colliding energy, and properties of the colliding nuclei. To gain a deeper understanding of these elements and possible effects of quantum chromodynamics in high-energy situations, researchers need a comprehensive picture of when and how different particles are created. This study uses data from Xe-Xe collisions at the LHC to provide precise information about when pions, kaons, protons, phi mesons, and other particles are produced, and compares these findings with similar results from Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC and Pb-Pb collisions at the SpS. The research shows that in Xe-Xe collisions, pions, kaons, and phi mesons were created within 0.6 to 1.8 fm, depending on the energy of the collision, and that the production of these particles was influenced by charges of the colliding nuclei but not significantly by energy charges. Furthermore, the research found that the most probable number of protons produced in Xe-Xe collisions ranged from 2.5 to 6.5, and that the production of these particles was influenced by both charges of the colliding nuclei and energy charges.

In late October 2019, violent protests and large-scale social unrest gripped Chile, severely impacting the country's healthcare system and posing significant risks to medical workers and patients. This study aims to explore a novel concept in epidemiology, where disease transmission is influenced by an individual's proximity to others who are distressed or experiencing trauma, in order to analyze the spread of psychological trauma and associated violent behavior. By applying this method, we used statistical data to reconstruct the dynamics of the protests and compared our simulation results with actual events, finding that a non-local approach can effectively model the spread of psychological trauma even when only accounting for the proximity of individuals who are participating in the protests. This phenomenon was particularly evident in the early stages of the protests. Furthermore, our simulations revealed that the protests' growth can be classified as exponential in the initial stages, and that the decline phase follows a power-law distribution with an estimated value of 1.83 for the protest's main hub. This research provides insights into the dynamics of the 2019 Chilean protests and offers a framework for studying the spread of psychological trauma and associated violent behavior.

This research focuses on an advanced version of regular expression constraints, extending traditional regular expression constraints to account for union and intersection operators, as well--for consistency reasons--excluding intersection results in an additional condition on the strings it should match or exclude from matching. We have developed a concise and precise mathematical representation of these constraints and demonstrated the feasibility of applying the principles of regular expression matching to this extended version, including identification of patterns not present in the input data and efficient computation of the results of matching against a set of input strings or patterns. We have further established the relationship between these extended constraints and regular languages defined by finite automata and, for completeness reasons, described the version excluding intersection. For the extended version, we have also established necessary and sufficient conditions for equivalence with regular expression constraints, as well as a method for resolving equality constraints and a method for determining whether a string matches a constraint, both of which can be accomplished using finite automata.

Mobile agents such as drones and robots are limited by the availability of visual data, as they often operate in environments with obstructed views, yet can access 3D terrain through their inertial sensors. To address this, we developed an automatic navigation method, capable of utilizing visual and inertial data in a way that accounts for the properties of each sensor. Invented was a novel attention-based mechanism, the Visual-Inertian Oblivion (VIO), which causes the system to ignore areas of the image that are less relevant to the navigation task at hand. Furthermore, to process sequential navigation data, we created a recurrent version of VIO, which we integrated into a state-of-the-art architecture. In multiple outdoor experiments on a drone equipped with a visual-inertial sensor, our navigation system demonstrated significant improvements over the current state-of-the-art, particularly in areas with obstructed views.

We have developed a method to apply the Keldysh contour technique for a wide range of Weyl semimetals in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional spaces, allowing us to apply the random phase approximation consistently and accurately, even when there are multiple Weyl points. This technique can be applied to both clean and disordered Weyl semimetals and can be used in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional spaces. We have investigated the effects of interactions on the energy levels and fermion numbers in Weyl semimetals and found that in clean, two-dimensional Weyl semimetals, the energy levels become non-linear and the fermion numbers become correlated with each other. In clean, three-dimensional Weyl semimetals, the energy levels remain linear, but the fermion numbers become correlated with each other. We have also investigated the effects of interactions on the energy levels and fermion numbers in a two-dimensional Weyl semimetal with a square lattice and found that it can exhibit both non-linear energy levels and correlated fermion numbers, even in the absence of disorder. When disorder is present, it can exhibit the behavior of a topological Anderson insulator.

This paper presents a numerical method to solve the inverse problem of determining a function change in a part of a conductor, given the raw data of the conductor's boundary electric and magnetic fields, measured outside the conductor, assuming the field satisfies the time-dependent Maxwell equations and ignoring noise in the data. This is a model for the data completion problem in electrical impedance tomography. Uniqueness and stability of the solution for this problem are established under the assumption that the change occurs in a limited time period. A quasi-reversibility method is used to solve the numerical problem, and the algorithm and results are presented. Note that the case where the change varies with time is more difficult than the case where the change is time-independent and requires additional assumptions about the change and the measured data.

This paper addresses the challenge of combining disparate sources of
information in a federated setting, where data must remain on remote servers.
We focus on a fundamental operation, selecting and integrating data, which
is a crucial component for more complex tasks such as machine learning.
Given that participating servers may provide either selected or integrated
data, but not both, we must decide whether to accept pre-integrated data
risking suboptimal selection, or accept selected data risking suboptimal
integration.
Our key contribution is a straightforward and efficient approach to make
these decisions, enabling the incorporation of prior knowledge about the
integration quality.
In addition to this innovation, we offer a method to estimate the
expected value of pre-integrated data, which can be used to incorporate
the value of pre-integrated data into a utility function.
We empirically demonstrate the benefits of our approach in multiple
knowledge domains, including machine learning on a large and publicly
available data set.

We investigate the rank of elliptic curves defined over the rational numbers and extended to the Galois group $S_4$ and $A_4$ within the context of quartic extensions. It has been established that for a specific parameter $A$, the rank of an elliptic curve can be expressed as $0$ if $A$ is odd and non-squarefree, $2$ if $A$ is an odd square, $4$ if $A$ is an even square, and $6$ if $A$ is a multiple of $4$, all in the case of $S_4$-extensions. Furthermore, it has been found that the rank of an elliptic curve can be expressed as $0$ if $A$ is odd and non-squarefree, $2$ if $A$ is an odd square, and $4$ if $A$ is an even square, within the context of $A_4$-extensions. Notably, both results represent new findings.

A crucial boundary, the quantum focussking inequality, serves as a fundamental constraint in quantum gravity systems. Studies have shown that the QFI can be replaced by a more restrictive measure, the change in the quadratic part of the Rindler entropy, which serves as a speed limit for the change in the von Neumann entropy in Rindler time. In this research, we apply this more precise inequality to the entanglement near the edge (ENE) charge density in conformally coupled scalar field theories, both with and without a "holographic" counterpart in anti-de Sitter space. We found that in the absence of a holographic counterpart, the ENE charge density can exceed the ENE bound in Rindler time, leading to the onset of a period of rapid entropy decay during a phase transition known as the "relaxation" phase transition. In the presence of a holographic counterpart, we derived a more explicit formula for the change in the Fock-Rosenthal expansion of the Rindler entropy in Rindler time and verified that it adheres to the ENE bounds. We also applied this more precise inequality to a variety of holographic models, both with and without a "holographic" counterpart in anti-de Sitter space. Quantum systems, such as spin-1/2 particles, can be described using the Bloch vector, whose evolution is governed by the time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation and Heisenberg's picture, respectively. In this study, we examine the identifiability of a unknown time-dependent Hamiltonian from measurements of a spin-1/2 particle's state, and establish that it is possible to determine this Hamiltonian in a certain time frame, depending on the strength of the interaction. We also investigate two types of energy bounds that can be used to identify a unknown Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we develop a method to determine the minimum time required to identify a unknown Hamiltonian, along with associated confidence levels, and provide guidelines for implementing this in laboratory settings.

Let's consider the $\vee$-interpolation operator $I_\vee^{(n)}$ acting on polynomials of degree at most $n$ within the real number framework. A previously established bound suggests that the norm of this operator, when applied to a function $f$, is capped at a multiple of $n!$ times the norm of $f$.
However, our discovery shows that the correct multiple can be much smaller, specifically it is possible to set the constant at $2^{n+1}$ times the norm of $f$, which is a more precise estimate.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as a prominent platform for quantum computing, and to advance this technology, it's essential to address material issues at the breakdown point. Real-time analysis of defects within microwave resonators is crucial, yet detecting defects smaller than the wavelength poses a significant challenge. We've developed a method to overcome this difficulty by using a THz-sensitive technique, specifically lock-in terahertz scanning near-field holography. This technique allows for the non-invasively determination of carrier concentration and mobility at the nanoscale within planar microwave resonators. We've tested and demonstrated this method on microscale gold stripes and successfully applied it to a complex microwave resonator, uncovering a previously unresolvable defect with a diameter of approximately 200 nm.

The atmosphere of Venus underwent a prolonged process of oxygenation, which likely occurred over the course of several billion years as the planet's rate of volcanic gas release slowed. This atmosphere now contains nearly 2% oxygen by volume, although it's not suitable for supporting life due to the extreme heat and crushing pressure. We examine the possible sources of this oxygen, considering both biological and abiological origins, and evaluate the various reactions that maintain the balance of chemical elements and chemical composition of the atmosphere. We also investigate the atmospheric escape processes that broke down the initial oxygen-rich compounds and released free oxygen. Although the evidence is circumstantial, we propose that the current level of oxygen in the Venusian atmosphere is a result of interactions between endogenous processes, such as plate tectonics and biological activity, and exogenous factors like solar energy and cosmic rays. We conclude that the atmosphere of Venus eventually adopted a self-sustaining oxygen atmosphere as a result of a feedback loop where the release of oxygen gases led to the formation of an ozone layer, which in turn protected the atmosphere from being stripped of its oxygen by solar ultraviolet radiation.

To analyze point processes in their entirety, nonlinear Hawkes models serve as a
critical tool by inferring network structures and properties.
These models incorporate the characteristics of points occurring within a
timeframe and incorporate feedback, representing the effects of past events on
their own generation rates.
Despite their analytical benefits, many of their properties under non-strict
conditions remain unexplored, posing a challenge for their application in
real-world settings.
This paper provides a novel Bayesian parameter estimation method for nonlinear
Hawkes models based on the Gibbs sampler, including an algorithm for inverting
the Gram matrix and an efficient way to update the precision matrix in a
non-strict condition context.
Results from simulated data indicate the method's accuracy and a study on
event recordings from a financial news agency uncovers a nonlinear relationship
and reveals the directions of influence between events.

In highly intense laser plasmas, polarization can shift and a beam can become randomly oriented due to excessive reflection from turbulent plasma. This phenomenon can impede high-grade petawatt laser applications, especially those relying on high-energy pulses with a specific polarization. The intensity limits of this kind of polarization disruption and alteration have been studied in a model that incorporates both the effects of plasma electron scattering and the influence of a magnetic field on light propagation and interaction with plasmas. The results indicate that in plasmas with moderate densities and in the presence of a strong magnetic field, the degree of polarization can be maintained at higher intensities than previously reported, with the specific limit found to be in the range of $10^{21}$ W/cm$^2$ for $10$ $\mu$m laser pulses interacting with a plasma of density $10^{17}$ cm$^{-3}$, and this limit can be further increased by aligning the magnetic field with the laser wave vector.

Re-examining the data from Drell-Yan processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) with higher precision and newer techniques allows for a more detailed investigation of the distribution of the tau lepton's charge within its interior. By re-analyzing a substantial dataset from the ATLAS experiment, researchers have updated their understanding of this distribution, often referred to as the 'electric dipole moment' of the tau lepton, in multiple aspects. Compared to the original finding, the updated calculation yields an enhanced estimate of approximately 0.21 centimeters, with an associated error of 0.01 centimeters. Furthermore, the data indicates that the tau lepton's charge is likely distributed randomly and evenly across its interior rather than being concentrated in the lepton's center.

A code's rank distance decay rate can be minimized to achieve error resistance, especially in information transfer scenarios where decoding speed is critical. A significant issue with rank distance codes is the difficulty of identifying closest codewords, mainly due to the NP-hard nature of the underlying problem. As such, various relaxation methods have been proposed to find approximate codeword neighbors. This study examines two popular codeword decoding approaches, the Gaussian ball decoding and bounded rank decoding, and introduces a more efficient method, Gaussian ball bounded rank decoding. The study shows that for symmetric rank distance codes, this new method achieves a codeword distance decay rate of up to three times better than existing methods, and achieves this rate under specific conditions where the codeword distance decay rate is proven to be as low as two for all codewords.

Building upon the fundamental operators in CFT$_2$, we establish a comprehensive framework for defining spinning operator algebra in AdS$_3$. By applying the Miura transformation, we connect the operator product expansion (OPE) in CFT$_2$ to the boundary algebra in AdS$_3$, and in doing so, we identify the parent CFT$_2$ operators that give rise to specific boundary operators in AdS$_3$. Notably, we demonstrate how the Rehberg-Roy formula can be applied to determine the conformal Casimir effect in the AdS$_3$ boundary algebra, and in a related example, we calculate the spin-$s$ two-point function in CFT$_2$ as well as its image in AdS$_3$.

In 1970, Gelfand and MacPherson established a significant link between Pontrjagin classes and a specific construction involving the Grassmannian and the Chern character, thus generalizing their earlier result from 1969. We intend to demonstrate how their findings are connected to the characteristic classes of singular spaces and provide an alternative proof of their findings.

We investigated the photometric and spectroscopic characteristics of the SN II 2020jfo using a combination of data from various sources, including the ATLAS, PASTEL, TASTE, VPHOS, VLT, and WHT instruments, and analyzed its properties in the context of relevant empirical and theoretical evidence, ultimately providing a reliable explosion energy estimate for this SN II and shedding light on its underlying physical mechanisms.

To significantly increase the field of view in X-ray telescopes while maintaining the ability to pinpoint the source of variations, a novel concept has been explored by designing a multi-focal plane lobster-eye lens array with a 2x2 configuration. This array features four separate focal planes, each corresponding to one quadrant of the lens, and allows for the tracking of transients across a wide area by identifying the affected quadrant where the event occurred. A simulation using the ZEMAX software has validated the feasibility of this design by confirming that it meets the required specifications, including a 4.5 degree field of view, a plate scale of 1.7 arcsec per pixel, and the ability to accurately determine the position of point sources within a 10 arcsec radius from the optical axis. Furthermore, this design has been compared to a single large-format lobster-eye lens with a 2x2 tiling scheme, and it was found that the multi-focal plane design can reduce the optical aberrations and improve the resolution, although it requires a 2.5 times larger entrance pupil and results in a 25% loss of effective collecting area.

We modify the two-factor stage model to a version with a fixed set of possible factor values, and prove a new version of the partial uniform ellipticity property holds in this case. We also show either the market has no information about the second-factor, or it satisfies the conditions of the first-factor model with the partial uniform ellipticity property.

To explore the link between cosmic velocity and the mass of dark matter halos, a non-linear analysis is required, presenting a significant challenge for traditional methods. By applying a deep neural network to analyze the characteristics of dark matter halos from the IllustrisTNG simulation, researchers found that the influence of velocity on halo mass is minor, with a precise upper limit of 1.5 per cent, and primarily limited to very specific and rare scenarios.

We've reimagined the method for solving the Einstein-Newton system in the context of rotating stars, with a focus on formulating the problem using weighted vertical multi-domain grid methods and quasi-local energy-momentum relations. We've updated Emerici's formulation to better suit these needs and have confidence that any rotating star configuration can be accurately described using this new formulation. We've further determined that the specific relation defining the angular velocity can be chosen based on the desired accuracy in calculating the mass spectrum of rotating stars, with an emphasis on results obtained using the relativistic rotation equation of Grotier et al. We've tested this new formulation against a range of known numerical solutions and have found that by using the correct relation, the accuracy with which the system is solved can be significantly improved, with an example showing that the Limb-darkening coefficients calculated using this method agree with observations to within their error margins. We've also made available the computer code used in this study, in the hope that it may be useful to others working on related problems.

Recently developed document extraction models can automatically identify and extract data from complex documents such as invoices, but they require a substantial amount of labeled data to achieve high accuracy. In contrast, they can easily process a large number of unlabeled documents. Leveraging this imbalance, we propose an efficient approach called Targeted Batch Annotation (TBA) to minimize labeling costs. TBA selects the most uncertain and critical entries to label, based on an assessment of their importance and potential impact on overall project effectiveness. In order to determine the most effective strategy for TBA, we developed a simulation platform and tested it with multiple scenarios, achieving an average cost reduction of 80% while maintaining similar accuracy levels. In addition to TBA, we also explored and compared other labeling strategies and validated the usability of our approach with real-world data.

Recently, the observation of gravitational waves has become possible with the advent of LIGO and VIRGO technologies, allowing for a new method of using gravitational waves to study the universe, particularly in analyzing neutron star-black hole (NSBH) collisions. However, with millions of gravitational wave candidates detected annually, a high-speed classification system is required to process them in a short period, making a traditional machine learning method impractical. We present a new, efficient method of training a convolutional neural network (CNN) to identify three main components of gravitational waves and a separate recurrent neural network (RNN) to determine the binary component of a gravitational wave event, allowing for a compact and rapid classification of events. We demonstrate that it is possible to classify events correctly in as little as 0.25 seconds per sample, achieving an overall F1-score of 0.943. We also discuss the incorporation of raw data waveforms and additional astrophysical information into the classification model.

In this study, we investigate how urban residents' social interactions in Shanghai were affected by COVID-19 restrictions and resulting consequences on the city's economy. To achieve this, we analyze a survey of 1,000 local residents conducted in May 2020 and sort them into three categories based on their economic activity during the pandemic: those whose economic activity significantly decreased, those with a moderate decline, and those whose economic activity remained largely unaffected. We find that residents from the middle class in Shanghai, particularly those from the Yangtze River Delta's urban areas, exhibited distinct pandemic behaviors. Compared to their urban peers from other Chinese regions, they showed a greater tendency to reduce social interactions, adhere to pandemic protocols, and adopt risk-reducing economic strategies. These findings persist even after accounting for individual factors such as age, household income, and fear of pandemic consequences. Notably, we discover that middle-class urban residents from the Yangtze River Delta were more likely to decrease their social interactions even before the pandemic hit, and this pre-existing pattern contributed to the observed economic effects. Overall, our research reveals that the pandemic exacerbated existing income disparities in urban social interactions in Shanghai, and that these disparities can be addressed through targeted economic stimulus packages aimed at reviving the city's urban economy.

We present an analysis of 116 massive protostars in the early stages of their development, focusing on the growth of their central dense cores and surrounding accretion disks. By examining multiple-line density and temperature data, we were able to map the total mass of these cores and calculate the rates of accretion and mass growth. Our findings reveal that the growth patterns of these cores vary, with some experiencing rapid growth, while others experience more gradual growth. We also observe an peak in mass growth rates of around 10^-3 per year. Furthermore, we discovered an association between the formation of massive stars and the presence of nearby dense gas that can be targeted by submillimeter surveys, such as SHGB. Our study suggests that the development of massive stars involves the accumulation of mass over a prolonged period, with an average timespan of around 10,000 to 50,000 years. We also explored the possibility of dense cores merging with each other or with nearby clumps of gas, finding that while such mergers could contribute to mass accumulation, they do not significantly impact the overall patterns of growth we observed.

When operating in a channel with no bottom obstacles, a Hamiltonian formulation is now applied to a wide range of deep-water gravity waves with varying levels of accuracy, using the water surface height and velocity potential as variables. The Hamiltonian formulation leads directly to a system of partial differential equations that includes the Hamiltonian, the Hamiltonian vector field, and the conservation of two quantities - energy and wave number squared. The Hamiltonian formulation is then used to modify the Dysthe Hamiltonian, which in turn leads to a new set of partial differential equations, and by applying the Hamiltonian vector field to the double correlation function, it is possible to derive a new set of PDEs that match those obtained through a multiple-scale analysis, thus confirming the validity of the new formulation. The new formulation, referred to as the Hamiltonian Dysthe formula, reduces to the standard Dysthe formula when the wave nonlinearity and dispersion are weak, and it is applicable to waves with amplitudes up to 0.4 when using either the Hamiltonian Dysthe or the Hamiltonian Wigner formulations. The new formulation, the Hamiltonian Wigner formulation, the Hamiltonian Dysthe formula, and the Dysthe formula are compared by applying them to a step function initial condition, and it is also possible to derive the Hamiltonian Dysthe formula from the Hamiltonian Wigner formulation, using a change of variables. In dimensions two and higher, a concept called locally convex terrains has been given a significant advancement. It has been shown that a method similar to integration over a surface can be applied to these terrains. This result also leads to an expanded version of the Stokes theorem for these terrains. It has been further established that if a locally convex terrain in n-dimensional space has n-2 times differentiable edges, then it has a well-defined (n-2)-th order surface area, making the Stokes theorem valid for these terrains when the form of the theorem has an (n-2)-th order differential weight. It has been demonstrated that the standard parabolic terrains, defined by the intersection of n hyperplanes in n-dimensional space, can be used as a basis to expand the Stokes theorem to these terrains and also to polyhedron boundaries in n-dimensional space. It has been shown that if a locally convex terrain in n-dimensional space has n-1 times differentiable edges and is bounded above and below by n hyperplanes, then it has a well-defined (n-1)-th order surface area, making the Stokes theorem valid for these terrains when the form of the theorem has an (n-1)-th order differential weight. It has been further established that the Stokes theorem can be applied to the boundaries of polyhedra in n-dimensional space.
