Autonomous navigation in complex environments with multiple levels requires the integration of advanced technologies.  Our proposed method, which we call immediate sonar blending (ISB), utilizes a layered navigation framework to combine data from various heights.  By prioritizing and weighting scan data from different heights, ISB creates a unified, obstacle-free path for the robot to follow.  We tested ISB on a simulation model of a office building and found it to be highly effective, with a success rate of over 90% in finding a path through the space.  Our results also showed that the algorithm can handle a wide range of speeds and heights, and that the height weights it determines are consistent with the actual height of the obstacles.  Furthermore, ISB operates at a rapid pace, with an average computation time of just 21 milliseconds.

The prevalence of deceitful media reports poses a significant challenge for individuals and organizations in navigating the online world. As the quantity of published content keeps escalating, automated methods to identify suspicious media stories are crucial. One such approach involves utilizing language models to create concise versions of lengthy text, which can be trained to pinpoint deceitful media reports along with short summaries indicating their classification. In the present study, we apply a pre-existing dataset containing classified media reports, including summaries written by their own authors, to train a model in detecting deceitful media reports based on text summarization. In evaluating the proposed method, we compared it to existing techniques and found it to be either equal to or superior in accuracy, depending on the dataset used. Furthermore, we explored ways to reduce the complexity of the model, which resulted in a significant improvement in performance when evaluated on a different dataset. The proposed technique demonstrates potential in detecting deceitful media reports and identifying relevant summary features, which can be utilized for other text classification tasks.

Out of water, grains undergo a significant shift in behavior, transitioning from a fluid-like state to a solid-like state, a phenomenon known as grain bending that affects sound and visual properties, particularly in deep water environments where the angle of incidence is significant. Until now, research on this subject has been conducted using simple statistical models. In a breakthrough, we are the first to investigate the effects of grain bending using a more advanced random field method. This breakthrough allows for a deeper analysis of the relationship between the angle of the incident light or sound and the properties of the grains, and for the first time, we are able to study the effects of grain bending in three dimensions. Along with the development of a new theoretical framework, we also conducted an experiment to test the principles, using a laser to measure the angle of the grains at a university campus. The results of this experiment were then applied to a new mathematical model, and for the sake of completeness, we also included a discussion on the validity of the previous simple models.

To identify the primary direction of a data set whose orientation does not affect its physical properties, a new algorithm is proposed that utilizes gradient descent to optimize an objective function defined by the $\ell_1$-norm dot product, is computationally efficient and converges linearly to a stable solution under the condition of rotational invariance. The algorithm can be applied to data sets with an affine transformation or those satisfying a rotationally invariant distance criterion. A theoretical analysis of the algorithm's performance, as well as an alternative derivation of the objective function, are also presented. Experiments with real and synthetic data demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness.

Recently, annotated data has been successfully applied to train and evaluate emotional understanding in question answering.  However, due to the time-consuming and subjective nature of human annotation, revising and updating existing annotations can be difficult to accomplish at scale. A novel method is presented here to facilitate large-scale annotation revisions by leveraging a small set of initial annotations and machine learning models trained on large datasets. This approach first trains a BERT-based classification model using the existing annotations and then uses the model to reannotate and filter revised answers for further review by human annotators. Experiments using both Quora and Sema-MT datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in enhancing the accuracy of annotations and reducing reliance on costly human judgment.

For a robot to successfully navigate unfamiliar environments, it needs a robust mapping technique that can adapt to new data and efficiently guide its path. In the context of exploration and mapping with limited prior knowledge, a stable framework is crucial to prevent the map from becoming too complex and confusing. To address these challenges, a novel navigation system called HiTMap has been developed, featuring a unique topological representation that combines a hierarchical layout and mapping capabilities. This approach allows HiTMap to construct an initial graph with a minimal number of nodes and edges, which can then be expanded as the environment is discovered, without the need for re-computation. By utilizing an innovative method to determine the optimal order for adding nodes to the map, HiTMap prevents the creation of unnecessary connections that can confuse the system. Our experiments, conducted in various simulation settings and using the Gazebo and V-redundancy tools, demonstrate HiTMap's ability to efficiently navigate through unfamiliar environments with obstacle avoidance, compared to other popular navigation systems.

One of the most precise methods of of position measurement is atomic interferometry, which can detect atomic displacement as small as one thousandth of an atomic diameter. To achieve the most sensitive atomic displacement measurement, the original source atomic beam should be made up of two distinct atomic waves that overlap in a specific way. This results in a position measurement that is extremely sensitive to local changes in mass and electric potential. When using atomic interferometry to measure the change in a local magnetic field, the arrangement of atomic waves must overlap in a specific way that is sensitive to changes in the Earth's gravitational field or the motion of the atoms. By using atomic interferometry to measure the effect of a local magnetic field on atomic waves, researchers found that it was possible to detect a change in a local magnetic field as small as 0.17 millitesla. This is the most sensitive measurement of a local magnetic field achieved to date. This level of precision was also used to measure the strength of a local magnetic field in the vicinity of a superconductor, where the arrangement of atomic waves was affected by the minimal change in the motion of the atoms caused by the Meissner effect. This was the first time the superconductor's effect on the motion of atoms had been measured in this way. This achievement also marked the first time atomic interferometry was used to measure the change in a local magnetic field outside of a vacuum. In this context, we examine a mixture model as a means to integrate two distinct probability distributions through the application of a mixture rule. We then explore the geometric representation of this model, revealing its equivalence to a specific point in a particular polyhedral cone defined by linear inequalities. We demonstrate that this geometric formulation can be used to derive both parametric and nonparametric versions of Bayesian estimation methods. Additionally, we discuss the extension of this framework to models with an infinite number of component distributions. Our discussion is accompanied by numerical examples and an exploration of the theoretical foundations underlying this approach.

Developing high-performance object-oriented applications on the GPU for scientific simulations, such as molecular dynamics simulations, remains challenging due to inefficient memory access and management. Current approaches that use flat memory layouts can lead to significant fragmentation, hindering the effectiveness of GPU memory management. A new memory allocator, DynaSOAr, is presented that tackles these issues by offering a concurrent memory allocator for object-oriented development on the GPU. DynaSOAr employs a hybrid free-list strategy and a coalesced block allocation method to minimize fragmentation, improve memory reuse, and enhance the efficiency of GPU memory management. To further optimize memory access, DynaSOAr incorporates a particle indirect buffer size that adapts to the size of the object array, leading to improved performance by reducing unnecessary memory alignment. The results show that DynaSOAr achieves a 1.7 times performance improvement in a molecular dynamics simulation and a 2.3 times performance improvement in an N-body simulation on an Ampere-based GPU compared to existing approaches.

Initial principles methodology has been employed to develop a precise model of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states for a single magnetic impurity and a dimer based on Nb(110), with particular focus on a manganese adatom and manganese dimers located at a hatch pattern site. Utilizing a (1x1) surface unit cell, the band structure of the clean Nb(110) surface was calculated and showed good agreement with available experimental and theoretical data, exhibiting three distinct d-band lobes that correlate with different atomic planes. The YSR state calculations were performed using a relativistic version of the RMT-YSR method, incorporating strong correlation effects. Numerical results reveal that the YSR level shifts exhibit a linear relationship with both the local magnetic moment and the on-site energy, displaying a factor of ten difference in scaling. Furthermore, the spin-orbit coupling was found to influence the YSR level position by up to 10 meV, with an effect that varies with orientation, and was shown to account for previous experimental measurements of manganese adatom and dimer YSR levels on Nb(110).

The study of exoplanetary systems with multiple bodies around a single star can provide valuable insights into the formation and evolution of planetary systems. This study presents the detection of five confirmed transiting exoplanaries orbiting TOI-712, a 7500 K G-type star. The exoplanaries, with radii ranging from 22,500 to 31,000 km, have orbital periods between 14.5 to 63 days. The marginal residual polynomial indicated a fit for three-dimensional stellar oscillations, suggesting TOI-712 is a solar-like star rather than a sub-giant. The exoplanary masses were estimated to be between 20 to 40 Earth masses using the surface gravity technique, although this method is highly sensitive to the uncertainty of the stellar mass and radius. The exoplanary masses could also be calculated from the orbital parameters and the gravitational influence on the stellar oscillations, yielding values between 10 to 20 Earth masses with more precision. The exoplanary periods, semi-major axes, and surface gravity indicated they are mini-Neptunes rather than gas giants. The limited size difference between the inner and outer planets suggests their formation processes may have been closely linked. The exoplanary orbits maintain orbital stability due to the significant tidal dissipation of TOI-712, which likely results from its juvenile formation within a disk of gas and solid particles surrounding its parent star. We employed density functional theory to investigate the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen impurities in rutile titanium dioxide.  The results show that both elements can exhibit magnetic properties when embedded with a single positive charge, however the arrangement of their electrons and magnetic characteristics differs.  The magnetic properties of nitrogen can be more pronounced when it has a double positive charge, however this arrangement is associated with high energy levels and may not occur naturally.  The energy levels of both elements can be influenced by the location of the embedded atom within the titanium dioxide structure, with the bonding electrons being affected in a "piecemeal" manner as the embedded atom moves through the lattice.  Notably, both elements can exhibit magnetic properties as part of a doped lattice, even at a single charge, which is a previously unreported characteristic.

In searches for beyond the Standard Model physics, particularly beyond the elastic production of top quarks, the study proposes utilizing forward rapidity production of central rapidity jets in proton-proton collisions as a signature. This signature, which could indicate the scattering of massive vector bosplets, such as heavy Higgs bosons or massive dark force bosons, is examined using data from the Large Hadron Collider with an integrated luminosity of 300 inverse picobarns. To identify this signature, the study uses a method that prioritizes event elasticity, namely, the requirement that the transverse energy produced at the forward end be significant in relation to the energy of scattered protons. In this context, the study selects events in which the sum of jet transverse energy in the central region exceeds 250 GeV and the missing transverse energy is less than 50 GeV. In such cases, the study shows that the elastic potential of the process can be enhanced by at least a factor of 10 in comparison to inelastic production of top quarks, with event selection efficiencies of 0.1 to 10% for processes with massive vector bosplets in the mass range of 0.1 to 1 TeV.

An upper rich graph is defined as one in which every 2-coloring contains a monochromatic $K_r$ subgraph for some fixed r. This concept is equivalent to a specific high level of Ramsey behavior. In our research, we determined the minimum number r, denoted as $\mathcal{U}_\Gamma$, exhibited by an infinite, countably-vertexed subgraph $\Gamma$ as an upper bound for its richness, and we established that any countable, non-compact upper rich space must be isomorphic to a particular type of tree-structured partition, whose r values form a sequence that is both rapidly increasing and indicate the depth of the associated tree, and we also proved that $\mathcal{U}_\Gamma$ can be any r that is both sufficiently large and part of a specific class, which includes all numbers that are capable of forming a pair indicating a level of difficulty in identifying a specific type of r-sized graph, and demonstrated this by creating a method for which an input r can be used to construct $\Gamma$ whose $\mathcal{U}_\Gamma$ equals r.

We've developed a method to achieve quantum sound in 2D U(1) gauge theories at finite temperature and non-zero chemical potential in Qutrits, which are based on three-level atoms. By analyzing the results, we found that in the "symmetric phase", the distribution of "glueball" energies can be accurately described using a Boltzmann distribution. Furthermore, we investigated the effects of temperature, chemical potential, and beam characteristics on "glueball" formation and demonstrated that our proposal is feasible with the technological capabilities of ongoing and future trapped ion systems.

Recent research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced at high rates through interactions between a powerful laser and a thick foil rich in carbon, aluminum, or copper, specifically within the limits of QED effects. Utilizing the sophisticated GENESIS3 code, a new model is developed to analyze the dynamics of the electrons and photons in the context of relativistic electrodynamics. The code's ability to simulate the distribution of pair production through the Bessel functions of the first kind is particularly notable. By combining the results of these simulations with an analysis of the positron population, it becomes possible to gain insight into the generated pair distributions and the effects of QED, as well as the influence of the laser's intensity, the number of electrons, the density of the target, and the angle of the positrons. Moreover, this research demonstrates the potential for a specific arrangement of the POPPA II experiment to detect the unique characteristics of the polarized positrons emitted perpendicular to the plane defined by the polarization of the laser and the direction of the positrons' motion.

An important concept in algebra called the diameter has been examined in this paper, specifically for a particular type of algebra known as a finite group. Here, the researcher seeks to contribute a new upper limit to the diameter's value, which is directly tied to specific characteristics of the group's structure. These characteristics include the number of group elements, the number of subgroup combinations, and the number of unique subgroups themselves. Notably, this upper limit can be expressed in terms of particular mathematical functions and constants associated with the group in question. To illustrate this finding, both theoretical and practical examples of finite groups are provided. One notable example of a finite group is projective linear groups, which includes examples like $PSL(2,8)$ and $M_{11}$. To achieve this result, the researcher applied and combined various techniques and theorems from both number theory and geometry. One notable approach used here is the Cayley's permutation representation method. Moreover, this research can be seen as an extension to an earlier result related to diameter value shared previously by the same researcher. One interesting aspect of the diameter value is that it can be used to determine another group's property, specifically whether a finite group is soluble or not. One notable example of a finite group that falls into the soluble category is the symmetric group $S_n$, whereas an example of an insoluble group is the alternating group $A_n$. This research develops an innovative temperature detection microchip, capable of withstanding a broad operating voltage range of 1.8V and providing accurate temperature readings in a confined area of 0.24°C with an error of ±1.4°C over a range of -40°C to 100°C. The proposed design leverages a delta-sigma modulator and an analog-to-digital converter to achieve high precision in a compact footprint, utilizing only 0.021mm² of area. A unique feedback loop is implemented to enhance stability and minimize errors. A novel threshold detection method is developed to calculate body temperature in the range of 36.5°C to 37.5°C with an error of ±0.5°C. A sub-threshold temperature detection mode is also designed to conserve power by reducing operating voltage to 0.6V at the cost of increased area of 0.057mm². Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this design.

This research paper reinforces the concept that introduces a well-defined geometric framework, specifically a differentiable manifold, as requiring a surjective submersive subgerm of a specific dimension. We demonstrate how this definition can be applied to Lie groupoids and stacks with a focus on their underlying geometric properties. The notion of a weak morphism between Lie groupoids is also examined and its relationship with the pullback construction in the context of presheaves is explored. The paper's results can be found in an earlier study by the same authors, but it aims to provide a clear and concise explanation of the key concepts for the benefit of the mathematical community.

A protostellar core's growth into a massive star-forming core can be an critical phase in the life cycle of a core, however the lack of observed core growth at early stages hinders our understanding of this process. We examined the molecular structure and chemistry of the Barnard 67 dark nebula using multiple-line observations from the MOPRA, NRO, GBT, and IRAS, and found it to be a complex, three-dimensional object with both rotating cores and outflows, similar to other infrared dark cores. Notable features include a molecular gas mass of approximately 13.8 solar masses, a temperature of about 20 K, a HCN-to-CO abundance ratio indicative of core evolution, and a large, slowly rotating column of gas blocking the background radiation. We estimate the core's mass will likely produce either an O-star or a massive young stellar object.

Researchers have long been studying random geometric fields defined by points on the surface of a unit sphere with a Radon measure as their probability measure, often using Gaussian versions of these models. Despite the relative simplicity of these models, many of their important properties remain difficult to calculate directly. To overcome this challenge, researchers have been using the properties of a specific Gaussian model, based on a specific matrix norm, to their advantage. In our work, we are exploring the behavior of a specific model, where the locations of the points are determined by the action of a matrix on a normally distributed vector, with the matrix defined by the eigenvectors of a specific random circulation, and we are examining the recurrence of a specific Markov chain defined by these points. In our recent paper, we were able to show that a particular version of this model, with a covariance matrix defined by a specific random circulation, results in a Markov chain that is recurrent when the dimension of the space is two or higher. In our current paper, we are taking a step further in exploring the same model when the probability measure is given by a Bessel distribution, and we are able to show that a particular version of this model, with a covariance matrix defined by a specific random circulation, results in a Markov chain that is recurrent when the dimension of the space is two or higher, with some additional conditions applying when the dimension of the space is exactly two. The interaction between a liquid surface and an intervening layer of another liquid or a gas, particularly when it's roughened by a texture, significantly affects the behavior of the system. It influences capillary phenomena, the stability of the surface, and the movement of an object across the surface. We have carried out an in-depth study using an inclined plate to create a textured interface within a liquid foam and have derived a general expression that explains the relationship between the texture-induced increase in friction and the characteristics of the system. We have also identified the conditions under which the influence of the texture becomes more significant, and have demonstrated its impact on the movement of an object across the surface and the stability of the system. Furthermore, we have analyzed the effect of the texture on a liquid surface in the presence of an air-liquid interface using a bubble in a beaker as a model, and have observed the formation of a'stick-slip' phenomenon when an object is moved across the surface of the bubble.

We've conducted an anomaly-aware training method's deep learning analysis to improve the detection of unusual skin carcinomas in medical images. By incorporating an SNN-based descriptor, we developed a two-class classification system to effectively identify unusual samples, with the majority of abnormal samples classified as the first class. In the first class, the CMK-Net model's performance was enhanced, with a score of 0.85 in the anomaly-aware setting, and the prediction of unusual samples showed a 0.78 F1-score, with the proposed method extracting unusual skin carcinomas from usually misclassified areas, such as the dermo-epidermal junction structure.

A pattern of finger veins has been made stable in a Hele-Shaw cell by subjecting it to a rotational shear force. Unlike the typical scenario where the pattern of a sine wave becomes unstable, this phenomenon has been explained by showing that a specific condition known as the Neumann stability criterion is not met when the cell is at rest. A study on the behavior of a stationary finger in a rotating frame of reference revealed that the stability of the pattern of finger veins depends on the orientation of the cell in relation to the direction of rotation and can be described by a simple mathematical expression. A comparison has also been made with the results obtained when the cell is subjected to a periodic shear force, where the pattern of finger veins becomes unstable and the behavior of the pattern has been described as a function of time. The possibility of creating a long, undulating interface between two fluids with a significant difference in density has been discussed as an application of this research.

Astronomers used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array to conduct a detailed survey of ethynyl cyclopentadiene, a rare molecule, in the TMC-1 region. As a result, two previously unknown variants of this molecule were identified: C$_3$H$_3$N=CCH and C$_3$H$_3$C$\equiv$NCN. The ethynyl cyclopentadiene and its two variants are spatially distributed in a similar manner. The column density of the ethynyl cyclopentadiene variants was calculated to be $1.2 \times 10^{11}$ g/cm$^2$, which is roughly 2.5 times the column density of cyclopentadiene. The abundance of the two variants was found to be nearly the same, with the cyclopentadiene derivative of cyanoacetylene being the most abundant molecule in the TMC-1 region. The ethynyl cyclopentadiene and its two variants likely originated from a carbon-rich environment with a low oxygen content. The ethynyl cyclopentadiene and its two variants are resistant to destruction and likely formed through the reaction of a cyclopentadiene molecule with a carbon atom. The abundance of the two variants can be used to test chemical models of the TMC-1 region.

In neural machine translation, the source and target texts are typically arranged in the same order, which simplifies attention models. However, this linear correspondence may not always hold in neural machine translation with sequential input output, such as text-to-speech and machine translation with out-of-order inputs, where the attention model must be able to navigate non-linear relationships between input and output elements. To address this challenge, we propose a novel look-forward attention model that infers the optimal reading order of the input elements based on the output sequence, and uses this order to compute attention weights. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model by incorporating it into neural machine translation systems for speech generation and machine translation with non-linear input outputs, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

The widespread adoption of grid computing was hinderly dependent on the success of a translation occurring between two distinct technological domains: the realm of scientific computing and the business world of distributed systems. This translation, carried out by the NorthGrid team, resulted in a well-functioning grid computing system, capable of being readily implemented in various settings such as universities and businesses. In the aftermath of the Singapore Grid Application Workshop, a surge in interest in grid technology became apparent, leading to an uptick in project proposals related to grid computing. One such project, developed by the NorthGrid team, utilized a grid computing setup to manage workload distribution and optimize performance among various nodes, demonstrating the practical applicability of the technology. In the paper, we outline the architecture of the NorthGrid system and detail the issues faced during its development, including difficulties with job scheduling, security measures, and performance optimization, as well as the solutions that were found to address these challenges. The NorthGrid system was subsequently integrated into the Singapore Grid Workshop's own infrastructure, further cementing the translation of the technology.

In this work, we develop a novel cosmological model where both dark matter and dark energy follow a combined dark fluid dynamics, and we conduct a detailed mathematical analysis of the model's parameters, 'de Sitter' expansion phase, equilibrium state, and the 'acceleration' era, specifically within a FRW metric framework. We also investigate the sound waves of the combined dark fluid and derive the modified Poisson equation for the model. Furthermore, we apply the combined dark fluid model to explain the observed 'acceleration' era of the cosmos and conduct an analytical examination of its Chapman series expansion.

J/ψ particles can decay into photons and invisible matter, and measurements of the decay width can provide important constraints on theories that include neutrino oscillations and dark energy. By calculating the J/ψ invisible decay width in the Standard Model with its own built-in neutrino oscillations, we find that this width can be expressed in terms of the neutrino oscillation probability, which can be determined using other J/ψ decay modes. We also calculate the contribution of the neutrino oscillation effect on the J/ψ invisible decay width and find it to be very small. In the context of dark energy, we investigate the effects of the J/ψ invisible decay width on the effective potential for the Higgs field and find that it is minimal when the J/ψ invisible decay width is large. We discuss two approaches to interpreting the J/ψ invisible decay width: a direct method and an indirect method, which can be used to determine the neutrino oscillation probability. We estimate that the J/ψ invisible decay width at the energy frontier could be anywhere from a few GeV to a few hundred GeV, and we discuss the possibility of measuring this width using initial J/ψ energy spectra.

Recently, research in singularity patterns of functions defined across multiple dimensions has gained significant interest, as evident from its growing presence in conference proceedings and publications. Recent studies in neuroscience are motivated by this trend and investigate the independent components of brain activity functions defined across spatial and temporal dimensions, employing a method called multivariate functional independent component analysis, whose corresponding algorithm includes a step called multivariate functional singular spectrum decomposition. To enhance the accuracy of the corresponding reconstruction results, the accuracy of the independent components is assessed and an improved algorithm is proposed, along with the introduction of a criterion for evaluating the number of components, and a joint estimation method for the parameters and components. The proposed approach is tested and compared to the existing method, and its effectiveness evaluated. Notably, this paper provides explicit formulations for the matrix differentiation and the multivariate functional independent component analysis algorithm, filling an existing knowledge gap. The research is applied to the analysis of brain activity data, providing a data preprocessing guide and a set of default parameters, along with graphical representations of the results, and openly shares the code on GitHub.

The long-term behavior of random walks in one dimension is well understood and leads to the Brownian motion evolution for most walks, except those that terminate within a finite time period known as the "recurrent" walks. In this study, we examine the relationship between the probability of a walk ending within a given time frame and its expected duration until the end. We achieve this by creating a threshold-based bound which contributes to the existing strategy for determining the expectation of the stopping time. Another approach uses the probability of the walk ending in a finite time as an indicator of its recurrent status. We also explore and analyze specific examples, including the standard random walk, the voter model, and the birth and death process.

The IShTAR plasma source, a key component for the W7-X stellarator, has been analyzed to understand its plasma behavior during the helicon phase. A combination of numerical and experimental methods was used to validate the plasma's properties and has shown that the plasma's non-localized electric field results in a double-layer structure, which causes the plasma's density to decrease in the plasma center. This decrease in density is responsible for the formation of a plasma "pinch" and could be mitigated by adjusting the plasma's length. Furthermore, the plasma's properties were found to be independent of the plasma chamber's wall condition, which is crucial for the IShTAR design. The experimental results were validated through the application of two asymptotic theories, the helicon double-layer (HDL) model and the helicon plasma theory, which provided a deeper understanding of the IShTAR plasma's behavior and confirmed the reliability of the source's design.

In histopathology images, pinpointing and extracting nuclei is a crucial step in automated analysis, which can aid diagnosticians in their work. To achieve this, a common technique is object detection used in conjunction with segmentation. However, this task faces significant challenges, primarily due to the limited and distorted training data resulting from manual annotation processes. To address this issue, a new method known as W-Net has been proposed, featuring an asymmetric structure with a focus on capturing complete objects before moving on to detailed analysis. The model was evaluated on two datasets for nucleus segmentation, demonstrating its superior performance in comparison to existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, experiments were conducted to investigate the impact of using transfer learning, which showed that pre-training the model on the CAMEL dataset prior to using it on the VHF dataset leads to a notable improvement in performance. W-Net's source code has been made available online for public use.

Let's consider a prime number p, a finite field F with p elements, and the absolute Galois group G of the rational number. For simplicity, let's denote the absolute Galois group of F as H. We are looking to prove that there is a surjective geometric morphism $\mathcal{X}_G \to \mathcal{X}_H$ between the associated geometric Grothendieck's simplicial topoi, where $\mathcal{X}_K$ represents the absolute Galois module $\mathrm{Gal}_K$ from [Sim17, Def. 2.1] for fields K with a finite characteristic and the property of being algebraically closed. In particular cases where the characteristic of the field is not two or three, this result can be derived from [Del87, Thm. 0.3]. Additionally, for the special linear groups in characteristic two or three, a weaker form of this theorem was established in [Del87, Thm. 0.3]. Moreover, for the special linear groups in characteristic two or three, a weaker form of this theorem was established in [Del87, Thm. 0.3]. Furthermore, this result can be applied to the automorphism groups of binary nonary forms in the fields with a finite characteristic.

Deep learning techniques, particularly graph-based methods, have achieved high levels of accuracy in intricate tasks such as social network classification and chemical compound prediction, but the underlying principles of these models remain poorly understood for many applications, with limited analysis available beyond basic mathematical structures. In an effort to address this knowledge gap, our study applies analytical signal processing tools to graph neural networks, transforming their trainable components into displacement domain filters that match the underlying data, and transforming their nont Trainable components into displacement domain kernels, with the goal of gaining insight into the underlying mechanisms of these models, with the potential to aid in the design of novel architectures, to provide a framework for analyzing the effects of hyperparameter choices, to aid in the selection of graph neural networks over alternative models, and to aid in the transfer of learned features between different datasets.

In a gravity theory that includes a complex scalar field, a modification can be made to add a term to the action, specifically with a Chern-Simons action for both the complex scalar field in relation to U(2) and the Einstein gravity in relation to U(d), which results in the formation of rotating black holes and solitons at all spins. The model can be expanded to include matter fields and gauge forces, using a certain cosmological constant, which can be either positive, negative, or zero. The complex scalar field arrangement can vary, with options for charged and complex scalar fields, as well as with and without symmetry, which affects the field's configuration and stability in both the black hole and soliton forms. The complex scalar field can also exhibit both massive and massless properties, which influence the hole's and soliton's characteristics, including their temperature, entropy, and stability. The theory can be tested through the analysis of rotating black hole solutions using Godel metrics and rotating soliton solutions using the monopole metric, which provide insights into the field's behavior and the cosmos' evolution.

This paper presents a novel Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) technique to accurately determine the elastic properties of soft tissues in real-time ultrasound elastography. In synthetic aperture techniques, the origin is typically considered as the transducer, but this assumption can lead to significant errors in displacement estimation, particularly with closely spaced elements. We have developed a VOSA method that takes into account the precise location of elements and their corresponding wavefronts to determine the source of each pulse-echo signal, allowing for the construction of a precise aperture that accurately estimates the lateral displacement. We have tested the VOSA method using both numerical and experimental data, with results showing that it can accurately determine the precise location of elements and their corresponding wavefronts to determine the source of each pulse-echo signal, allowing for the construction of a precise aperture that accurately estimates the lateral displacement with a mean error of 0.35 mm. We have also compared the VOSA method with the conventional synthetic aperture technique and found that it can significantly reduce the error in displacement estimation to 0.17 mm, with a speedup of 2.5 times in data processing.

Our proposed method, we create a new framework where a logical expression is used to describe a sequence of actions, which can be executed on a simulated environment, and not a game's reward or observation. This results in the possibility of multiple possible pseudocodes for the same task, but our algorithm selects the most precise one. We demonstrate the potential of our approach by applying it to challenging levels in the Super Mario Bros. game, where it achieves better results than existing methods.

In the context of high-dimensional data, the $k$-means clustering algorithm has a significant issue: it can result in data points being assigned to clusters based on the characteristics of the data's transformation, rather than its original features. Our research addresses this challenge by developing an efficient and effective algorithm for dynamic data clustering in $d$ dimensions, with only a near-optimal choice of parameters and without assuming that the data follows a specific distribution. In particular, we show that for data that varies over time and is represented in $d$ dimensions, our algorithm can choose the optimal parameter $k$ and minimize information distortion within a factor of $O(\sqrt{d})$ when the data remains unchanged, and a factor of $O(k \cdot \min\{d, \log t\})$ when it changes over time. We have created algorithms for solving this problem in both centralized and decentralized settings, along with our methods for achieving these results in the centralized context and a new decentralized co-ordination mechanism called the "Draw-Winner-on-Top" (DWT) algorithm.

In a recent study, a dynamic pursuit-evasion model with multiple agents was examined, and a hierarchical framework for designing policies for all levels of difficulty was established [1]. In the proposed framework, a hierarchical division of a stochastic environment was defined, and the challenge it presents was quantified as the expected payoff for the pursuers or the expected payoff for the evaders in a two-agent setup. The study showed that better-performing policies could be obtained through a grid search of parameter spaces within this hierarchical framework. Now, the paper at hand explores the application of this framework to a setup with three agents, where one pursuer and two evaders compete against each other. It also examines the findings from conducting a grid search to determine the parameters of a stochastic model of a parking lot, as well as the effects of these parameters on the hierarchy of the competition.

To analyze lepton collisions at high-energy levels, it is crucial to accurately measure the properties of vector bosons, particularly W bosons, in the presence of multiple protons scattering. This research focuses on developing an efficient method to determine the distribution of W boson rapidity and transverse mass by using two muons with minimal background, primarily produced by scattering processes involving multiple protons. To apply this analysis to actual data, it is essential to have a precise understanding of scattering patterns, local energy densities, and multiple scattering effects. To achieve this, we have developed three independent methods to calculate W boson properties based on colliding muon energies, all of which have been implemented in a comprehensive framework suitable for large-scale simulations.

In complex environments, robots often face numerous challenges that require them to perform multiple tasks simultaneously, as seen in scenarios like navigating and object manipulation. To achieve this, they must integrate information across various levels of their cognitive processes, starting from sensory inputs to output controls. A key challenge in this integration is avoiding destructive interference that can occur when different learned components of the system, such as neural networks, are trained together, leading to a focus on simple separate training and complex combined execution. In our work, we explore a more structured approach, using a modular architecture where knowledge is shared among the components of the network, and we investigate how this affects the performance of a specific model-based multi-task reinforcement learning system. Our key finding is that in a system with knowledge-based interaction, the shared knowledge acts to prevent destructive interference, primarily in a way that is dependent on the level of novelty in the state visited during testing. We validate our approach by applying it to a range of challenging multi-task problems, including those generated by the MuMu dataset and a manipulation task with novel states.

In 1949, Elbert Wheeler wrote an article for The Saturday Evening Post, titled "The Automaton", which featured a student struggling to understand his mathematics teacher, Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Kleene, and eventually a self-replicating automaton. We will examine the popular science history surrounding the "diagonalization lemma" and explore its connection to the "Liar paradox". We will also examine the statement and proof of the fixed-point theorem, as well as the self-replicating automaton constructed using this theorem. Additionally, we will discuss the relationship between the fixed-point theorem and the "Turing complete" concept, and provide a straightforward proof of the theorem.

This paper formulates the three spheres theorem for non-zero solutions to the Dirac-Helmholtz equation in $\mathbb{R}^3$, providing a generalization of a well-known result by H. Begehr and his collaborators.

InInverse Issues represents a research paradigm where prior information is combined with observed data to determine possible prior data, a process known as posterior extraction. A novel framework, referred to as Posterior Extraction via Conditional Adversarial Networks (PECAN), is proposed to automate this process. PECAN utilizes a non-symmetric conditional generative adversarial network to generate the posterior distribution and incorporates a regularization term to ensure consistency with prior information. To evaluate the proposed method, two inverse issues were used: removing confounding variables in causal learning and extracting latent variables in generative models. The results show that PECAN outperforms existing methods in both applications. Causal Adversarial Learning (CAL) was used to evaluate the method in a controlled environment, and showed that it could correctly remove confounding variables with a success rate of over 90%. On the other hand, the result of PECAN in the Generative Adversarial Learning (GAN) setting was compared to the original condition, with a result of 61.09% ± 10.69% being obtained for accurate reconstruction of the latent variables.

This article proves that any surface that remains unchanged under the flow of a particular dynamical system cannot be a level set of a specific function unless it is already known to be constant over the system's parameters. The validity of this result holds if the surface in question has a specific geometric property called positive curvature. The results mentioned here were initially established by the authors in 2019 and 2020, respectively. The article also reviews some of the earlier results on this topic, including those by Shafekh, Berster, and Hillen, as well as a third result related to the heat equation, also established by the authors in 2020. The article's results can be applied to certain types of partial differential equations, such as the Burgers equation and the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation. The article also includes an observation about the relationship between the surface's invariance and the system's characteristics, as well as an anisotropic version of one of the main theorems. The interstellar medium is comprised of complex, scattering material within the solar system and beyond. This material includes turbulent plasma that can cause astronomical signals to scintillate as they travel through space. Pulsar scintillometry, the study of this scintillation, offers a valuable tool for exploring the interstellar medium and can provide information on the plasma properties, the position and motion of the scattering material, and the phase shift of the scattering medium. By analyzing the scintillometry of pulsar B1133+16, researchers have gained insights into the plasma properties, including the temperature and density of the scattering material. They have also determined the line-of-sight component of the Earth's velocity relative to the scattering medium and have estimated the angle of the scattering medium's normal vector with respect to the line of sight. Furthermore, they have used polarization data to identify the location of the scattering material and have gained a more detailed understanding of the interstellar environment surrounding the pulsar.

To break through the 10-second speech generation limitation in TTS and the 6-second text-to-speech waveform generation limitation in WPMTS, we propose a new model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, which combines the benefits of WaveNet and pitch-sensitive WaveNet. This model maintains the same number of WaveNet's conditional layers as its input sequence length but reduces the number of dilated convolution layers in each conditional layer to two, allowing for faster and more efficient training. In the pitch-sensitive WaveNet components, we experiment with different numbers of dilated convolution layers to find that three is the optimal number, which is then used in our QP-Wavenet. Our QP-Wavenet achieves state-of-the-art INDEGO results in zero-mean WPMTS and demonstrates superior quality and naturalness in TTS, surpassing the reference model WaveNet-Tacotron, by achieving an MMDI score of 4.67 compared to its 4.59.

In the context of bicategories, we have a defined concept of shadows, which corresponds to the idea of combinatorial pseudo-functoriality. In a specific bicategorical framework, we find that shadows coincide with the notion of a specific type of graph-related operator, which can be used to determine the relationship between a pair of strings and a pair of shadows. This operator has a significant property: it is invariant to the order in which it acts on the strings. When applied to the simplest type of shadows, this operator yields the well-known Faddeev-Takhjtajan \tau-function, or rather, a modified version of it, which we call the shadow \tau-function. The relationship between the shadow \tau-function and the original Faddeev-Takhjtajan \tau-function can be expressed through the use of a specific change-of-variables, which can be obtained by means of a particular type of combinatorial transformation. The process of obtaining the shadow \tau-function can also be interpreted through the use of a specific kind of graph-related operator, which can be seen as a form of the Birkhoff normal form, in a setting that mirrors the classical context of Hamiltonian mechanics. Researchers studied how individuals with visual impairment navigate indoor environments by localizing auditory signals in real spaces, using a sound source localization method with two speakers, and analyzed factors such as the layout of the environment, the movement of the subject, and the timing of the sound, to determine their impact on localization accuracy, and the results showed that those with visual impairment accurately determined the relative positions of sound sources in relation to themselves, but had difficulty with absolute localization, and the findings are expected to guide the development of effective navigation assistance technology.

Recently, graph neural networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable performance in various tasks, however they are typically developed under the Euclidean distance, which may not accurately reflect the complex relationships in many real-world datasets, particularly those described by the Lorentzian distance. In an effort to address this limitation, we introduce a novel GNN architecture, Lorentzian GNN, which leverages Lorentzian distance in its neighborhood definition and learns a non-linear transformation to calculate node representations. We prove that Lorentzian GNNs minimize the empirical risk and ensure the network's capacity, and through extensive experiments, we demonstrate its superiority over current GNN methods in tasks involving biological and technological datasets described by the Lorentzian distance.

This research aims to identify the origins of a sound wave, assuming it has been detected and its propagation path is known. The problem is set within a static fluid in an infinitely extended domain, containing an object with a specific shape, and involves the minimization of a functional that represents the squared error between the detected sound and a calculated sound resulting from a hypothetical source at an unspecified location within the fluid's boundary, subject to the constraint of a fixed amount of movement in the solid object. Using the shape derivative method, the functional is shown to be minimized when the fluid's velocity in the solid object's boundary meets specific criteria, and this condition can be used to find the source that generated the detected sound wave.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model, tailored to the
empirical spirit of the Tsallis entropy, by incorporating an inhomogeneous
exponential decay, whose parameters vary with time. We derive the subjective
probability distribution associated with this model, using the Tsallis exponential
distribution as a reference. We also investigate the implications of this model
on existing theories, revealing that it encompasses the hyperbolic discounting
model, while offering distinct predictions amenable to experimental verification.

Recently, a novel gauge that achieves harmonic symmetry was proposed within the context of four-dimensional linearized gravity. By conducting an in-depth analysis of the Lorentzian harmonic gauge fixings, including both their mathematical representations and the associated ghost fields, we have a better understanding of how the choice of gauge affects the behavior of the graviton in both the classical and quantum realms. In the process of our investigation, we derived explicit expressions for the Lorentzian harmonic Riemann tensor contractions and explored the renormalizability of the Lorentzian harmonic gauge fixings. We also examined the Lorentzian harmonic gauge with a non-compact gauge group, which leads to the appearance of a mass term in the pure linearized gravity scenario, but found that this does not affect the renormalizability of the full linearized gravitation theory. We concluded that the Lorentzian harmonic gauge with a compact gauge group proves renormalizable, in the sense that the action on the operator level is invariant under the change of unitary operators, which are infinitesimally close to the identity. We also examined the Lorentzian harmonic gauge with a non-compact gauge group in the pure linearized gravity scenario and found that it behaves in the same manner as the Feynman gauge.

For a general quadratic Hamiltonian, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols using a change of variables, results in a set of canonical equilibrium conditions represented by a non-negative Hermitian matrix in a Weyl-Wigner representation. The matrix elements characterizing the canonical equilibrium state can be extracted through a diagonalization process of this Hermitian matrix in a unitary matrix, whose elements are the transformed Weyl-Wigner symbols of the canonical equilibrium conditions. The original Hamiltonian can be re-expressed in terms of these transformed Weyl-Wigner symbols, providing a local expansion that includes both the fluctuations of the Hamiltonian from the energy levels and the energy shifts from the thermal average, which are distinguished by a second-order unitary transformation. The distinction between these fluctuations and shifts is shown to be the source of the often-misinterpreted meaning of the Weyl-Wigner symbol of the Hamiltonian, which has been variously misinterpreted as representing the energy shift, with some considering it significant at thermal equilibrium, but it actually varies with the choice of thermal ensemble used, ultimately being a ensemble-dependent quantity that depends on the choice of thermal ensemble, indicating that the energy shift is both thermal and ensemble-dependent, which can be either positive or negative, indicating it represents the distance from the lowest energy level, rather than a positive energy shift.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been theoretically established since the 1940s and has been experimentally confirmed in various systems, including atomic gases, ions, and solids, as well as in quantum many-body scenarios. We examine the mathematical representation of a negative temperature state and discuss its statistical and thermodynamic properties. We also explore the relationship between negative temperature and the total energy of a system, and discuss the conditions under which negative temperatures become relevant in both closed and open systems. We then review the associated phenomena, including negative specific heat, population transfer, and emission enhancement, and highlight some potential applications, including the development of highly efficient lasers and the improvement of quantum memory performance. We conclude by acknowledging the limitations of our analysis and the need for further research into the dynamics of negative temperature systems.

To investigate the implications of a "dark force" on electroweak symmetry breaking, we've developed a new "scoto-seesaw" framework that applies to a minimal and general situation. In this context, we examine the compatibility of a certain "scoto-seesaw" scenario with Weakly-Interactive Massive Particles (WIMPs) as a dark matter theory and the stability of the Higgs vacuum. We've established a parameter region that meets both conditions and found that it's in line with other "dark force" descriptions that include a "dark" $SU(2)_L$ sector with three doublet WIMP fields. We've also considered the effects of this "scoto-seesaw" framework on the Higgs mass eigenstates and other relevant observables. To make this analysis more concrete, we've applied this "scoto-seesaw" framework to a specific "dark force" description, namely a minimal dark $SU(2)_L$ sector with a singlet-like dark matter field. In this case, we've updated the existing predictions to include the latest LHC data and SPHinx or "Scoto-Petese-Higgs" effective theories, and found that the latest LHC constraints limit the accessible parameter space to above 100 GeV. We investigate the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ orbital mixing in a generalized gradient approximation plus $U$ method within a $d^1$-$d^6$ electron configuration for 4d and 5d transition metal compounds, focusing on the relevant energy range from 0 to 5 eV around the Fermi level with Fermi surface topology in mind. Orbital mixing increases with decreasing $d$-electron count and shows a significant dependence on the exchange correlation potential. Notably, we find that the degree of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be substantial, with values of up to 1.5 eV, which is crucial for understanding the localized versus itinerant behavior in these compounds. Furthermore, we analyze the effects of orbital mixing on band shapes, addressing a common assumption that $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ bands can be distinguished based on their widths alone. Our results also imply that the often-used cubic crystal field parameterization may not be sufficient, and we suggest an alternative method using the total density of states as a reference to determine the energy levels of individual orbitals, which can help account for the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing and its spatial variation within the compound.

We investigate the connection between the topological properties of certain complex varieties, specifically their Chow rings, and the topological properties of transformed varieties resulting from certain types of changes, or alterations, inspired by the concept of relative Milnor fibration. These changes, or alterations, are specifically "relative" to a subvariety within the parent variety and can be thought of as a generalization of the type of changes that occur through the Milnor fibration. 

We examine the changes, or alterations, that occur in the context of varieties with rational attributes, focusing on the behavior of varieties with attributes related to Diophantine properties, such as varieties associated with quadratic forms, varieties defined by polynomial equations with coefficients from a field that includes the rational numbers, and varieties linked to elliptic curves. 

We also explore the changes, or alterations, that occur in the context of varieties with attributes related to geometric properties, focusing on the behavior of varieties with attributes related to singularities, such as varieties with isolated singularities and varieties with rational attributes in a broader sense, as well as varieties defined by polynomial equations with coefficients from a field that includes the rational numbers, and varieties linked to elliptic curves.

The accuracy of chest X-rays interpretation holds significant potential for enhancing pandemic management and preventing flu-related deaths. Deep learning-based methods in 2020 achieved an impressive 83% accuracy in identifying 13 common conditions, however these results can be influenced by various biases including those stemming from data and image characteristics. Such biases can lead to poorer performance when models are applied to images from different sources, a common occurrence in real-world settings where images originate from diverse platforms, were captured at different angles, include various levels of quality, and were taken under different respiratory cycle phases. In this research, we explore the potential for training models using images that account for these factors, and present an initial analysis of image attributes that influence model performance, and a preliminary strategy for selecting image features to include in training data. These findings can serve as the groundwork for future studies on more complex topics, such as the effect of capturing images during different respiratory cycle phases on model performance, and the development of more effective training data creation methods.

ViDaExpert is an application for visualizing high-dimensional vector data, with the ability to project it via nonlinear embedding methods such as t-SNE, with the option to switch between a full data set view and an in-depth examination of specific data points including their local structure and weights from the dimensionality reduction process. The application also allows for the calculation and display of similarities between data points, as well as the option to save and reload previously analyzed data points for further study. ViDaExpert runs on Windows and is available for download.
